overview:
The expression "Bhadrabahu traditions" refers to the complex web of sectarian narratives, textual attributions, pontifical lists, and regional memories that have grown around Ācārya Bhadrabāhu, the Jain patriarch revered as the last śruta-kevalin (knower of the complete fourteen Pūrvas) in both Digambara and Śvetāmbara lineages.

Across Jain traditions, Bhadrabāhu is remembered less as a single, clearly defined historical personality and more as a nodal figure at which questions of scriptural authority, monastic succession, and the north–south spread of Jainism converge. Digambara accounts emphasize his role as the fifth and last śruta-kevalin, successor to Govardhana Mahāmuni, and spiritual preceptor of Chandragupta Maurya, whose renunciation and death by saṃlekhana at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa are narrated in later southern texts and inscriptions.

Śvetāmbara traditions, by contrast, foreground Bhadrabāhu (often styled Bhadrabāhusūri or Ārya Bhadrabāhu) within the Sthavirāvalī (succession list of pontiffs) preserved in the Paryuṣaṇa-kalpa and related materials. Here he appears as a disciple of Yaśobhadra and teacher of Godāsa, Agnidatta, Yajñadatta, and Somadatta, with the Godāsagaṇa branching into four regional lineages in eastern India. In this northern strand, Bhadrabāhu is also associated—though not without scholarly dispute—with the authorship of the Kalpa Sūtra, a key Śvetāmbara canonical text describing the lives of Mahāvīra and other Tīrthaṅkaras and listing the early heads of the monastic order.

The Bhadrabāhu traditions therefore function as a bridge between Digambara and Śvetāmbara memory. Both sects agree on his status as the last śruta-kevalin, but they diverge on details of his teacher, disciples, travels, and literary output. Southern Digambara sources such as the Ārādhanā of Śivārya, Tiloyapaṇṇatti, Harivaṃśa-purāṇa, and the Dhavalā commentary, together with inscriptions at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa, construct a narrative in which Bhadrabāhu foresees a twelve-year famine, leads a migration of monks to the south, and becomes the pivotal figure in the early Jain presence in Karnataka. Northern Śvetāmbara sources, including niryuktis and cūrṇis on canonical texts, focus more on his place in the pontifical chain and the internal organization of the saṅgha.

Modern scholarship (for example, studies by M. A. Dhaky and Sagarmal Jain) has shown that these Bhadrabāhu traditions are layered, often conflating multiple acharyas bearing similar names and reflecting sectarian concerns of later centuries. Critical comparison of northern and southern sources reveals discrepancies in the names of his preceptor, disciples, and the chronology of his life, as well as uncertainty about which Bhadrabāhu, if any, authored specific niryuktis or the Kalpa Sūtra. As a result, contemporary historians treat Bhadrabāhu as a partly historical, partly hagiographical figure whose memory was repeatedly reshaped to anchor evolving Jain identities.

From a doctrinal perspective, the Bhadrabāhu traditions mark the perceived end of the era of complete scriptural mastery. The idea that Bhadrabāhu was the last śruta-kevalin underscores a consciousness of loss within the Jain community: after him, the Pūrvas and parts of the original canon are said to have gradually disappeared. This motif is shared across sects and becomes a key frame for understanding later efforts to codify, comment upon, and reconstruct Jain scriptures. In this sense, Bhadrabāhu is not only a person but also a symbol of the transition from an oral, fully remembered canon to a more fragmentary, textually stabilized tradition.

Regionally, the Bhadrabāhu traditions have left material traces in sites such as Chandragiri Hill at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa, where caves and memorials are associated with him and, in Digambara lore, with Chandragupta Maurya. These places serve as pilgrimage centers and visual anchors for narratives of migration, renunciation, and scriptural guardianship. At the same time, the coexistence of divergent stories about Bhadrabāhu in inscriptions, commentaries, and community education highlights the plural, anekāntic character of Jain historical memory: rather than a single fixed biography, there is a spectrum of Bhadrabāhu traditions, each reflecting the concerns of its time, region, and sect.

Taken together, the Bhadrabāhu traditions invite careful, source-based study. They show how Jain communities have used the figure of Bhadrabāhu to think about authority, continuity, and loss; how sectarian identities have been negotiated through competing claims about teachers and texts; and how historical criticism can coexist with devotional reverence. For students of Jainism, engaging these traditions means learning to distinguish between primary textual evidence, later hagiography, and modern reconstruction, while appreciating the enduring role of Bhadrabāhu as a shared, though differently interpreted, ancestor in the Jain monastic lineage.

primary_sources.title: Kalpa Sūtra (including Sthavirāvalī passages)
primary_sources.author: Traditionally attributed in Śvetāmbara tradition to Ārya Bhadrabāhu; modern scholarship treats the attribution as uncertain
primary_sources.original_text: Due to length and canonical status, the original Prakrit text is not reproduced here; see standard Śvetāmbara editions of the Kalpa Sūtra for the Sthavirāvalī sections that list Bhadrabāhu among the pontiffs.
primary_sources.transliteration: Examples of relevant sections are often cited as part of the "Sthavirāvalī" within the Paryuṣaṇa-kalpa recension of the Kalpa Sūtra, where names such as "Yaśobhadra", "Sambhūtavijaya", and "Bhadrabāhu" occur in sequence.
primary_sources.translation: In the Sthavirāvalī, Bhadrabāhu is presented as a disciple of Yaśobhadra and as the teacher of Godāsa and other monks, situating him within an early succession of heads of the Jain monastic order. These passages form a key basis for the Śvetāmbara memory of Bhadrabāhu as a white-clad (sthavirkalpi) monk and pontiff.
primary_sources.notes: This text belongs to corpus tier A (verified primary canonical text) in the Śvetāmbara tradition. The attribution of the entire Kalpa Sūtra to Bhadrabāhu is traditional and not universally accepted by modern scholars, who point to chronological and stylistic issues. The Sthavirāvalī itself is a layered list that evolved over time, and its references to Bhadrabāhu must be read critically in light of later redaction.

primary_sources.title: Paryuṣaṇa-kalpa and related Sthavirāvalī materials
primary_sources.author: Anonymous redactors within the Śvetāmbara canonical and ritual tradition
primary_sources.original_text: The Paryuṣaṇa-kalpa preserves a Sthavirāvalī in Prakrit listing pontiffs from Sudharmasvāmin onward. Bhadrabāhu appears in later phases of this list, with brief notices of his teacher (Yaśobhadra) and disciples (Godāsa, Agnidatta, Yajñadatta, Somadatta).
primary_sources.transliteration: Names and lineages are transmitted in Prakrit forms such as "Yaśobhadra", "Sambhūtavijaya", "Bhadrabāhu", "Godāsa", "Agnidatta", "Yajñadatta", "Somadatta", and the gaṇa and śākhā names "Tāmraliptikā", "Kotivarsīyā", "Paundravardhanikā", "Dāsīkarvatikā".
primary_sources.translation: The Sthavirāvalī records that Bhadrabāhu, of the Prācina gotra, was a disciple of Yaśobhadra and the teacher of four monks whose lineages spread to various towns in eastern India. These brief notices underpin Śvetāmbara accounts of Bhadrabāhu’s role in organizing the saṅgha and in the formation of the Godāsagaṇa and its branches.
primary_sources.notes: These materials are treated as corpus tier A–B (primary canonical text with early commentarial framing). Their evolution in phases has been analyzed by modern scholars, who distinguish earlier, shorter lists from later, more detailed ones. The presence of Bhadrabāhu in these lists is a central datum for northern Bhadrabāhu traditions, but the brevity of the entries leaves room for later hagiographical expansion.

primary_sources.title: Southern Digambara narrative and doctrinal texts (e.g., Ārādhanā of Śivārya, Tiloyapaṇṇatti, Harivaṃśa-purāṇa, Dhavalā)
primary_sources.author: Various Digambara authors, including Śivārya, Yativṛṣabha, Jinasena, and commentators on the Ṣaṭkhaṇḍāgama
primary_sources.original_text: These texts, composed in Prakrit, Apabhraṃśa, and Sanskrit, contain scattered references to Bhadrabāhu as a śruta-kevalin, as the teacher of Chandragupta Maurya, and as the leader of a migration to the south in response to a twelve-year famine.
primary_sources.transliteration: Passages refer to "Bhadrabāhu", "Govardhana Mahāmuni", "śruta-kevalī", and to the famine ("duvālasamvatsariya dukkha") and migration ("dakkiṇadesa-gamana") motifs, though exact wording varies by text and recension.
primary_sources.translation: In these southern sources, Bhadrabāhu is portrayed as the last śruta-kevalin who, foreseeing a twelve-year famine, leads a group of monks from Magadha to the south. Some narratives add that Chandragupta Maurya becomes his disciple, renounces his throne, and undertakes the fast of saṃlekhana at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa under Bhadrabāhu’s guidance. These stories link Bhadrabāhu to the early spread of Jainism in Karnataka and to the royal patronage of the Mauryan court.
primary_sources.notes: These texts range from corpus tier B (reviewed traditional commentary) to C (authoritative scholastic literature). The Chandragupta episode, in particular, is recognized by modern historians as hagiographical, lacking independent non-Jain corroboration. The famine and migration motif, however, is supported indirectly by epigraphic evidence of early Jain presence in southern India and is treated as a plausible, though not fully verifiable, historical memory.

primary_sources.title: Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa inscriptions and Bhadrabāhu memorials
primary_sources.author: Various donors and scribes; inscriptions compiled and studied by modern epigraphists
primary_sources.original_text: Kannada and Sanskrit inscriptions at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa mention Bhadrabāhu and, in some cases, Chandragupta, commemorating caves and basadis associated with their memory. The exact wording varies by inscription and date.
primary_sources.transliteration: Typical elements include names such as "Bhadrabāhu", "Candragupta", references to "muni", "saṃnyāsa", and place names like "Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa" and "Candragiri".
primary_sources.translation: These inscriptions record donations, constructions, and commemorations linked to Bhadrabāhu and Chandragupta, presenting them as revered figures whose austerities and teachings sanctified the site. They do not provide a continuous biography but attest to the strength of local tradition associating Bhadrabāhu with Chandragiri Hill and with the early Jain community in Karnataka.
primary_sources.notes: Epigraphic materials are treated as corpus tier A–C, depending on their date and preservation. They are crucial for understanding how Bhadrabāhu traditions were localized and materialized in southern India. At the same time, they reflect the state of memory at the time of inscription, not necessarily the historical reality of the 4th–3rd centuries BCE.

misconceptions.myth: There was only one historical Bhadrabāhu, and all texts and stories about "Bhadrabāhu" refer to the same person.
misconceptions.reality: Modern critical study of Jain sources shows that multiple acharyas named Ārya Bhadra or Bhadrabāhu were active at different times, and later authors often conflated their lives and works. As a result, not every text or narrative attributed to "Bhadrabāhu" can safely be assigned to the śruta-kevalin Bhadrabāhu of early tradition; some belong to other teachers with similar names or to later hagiographical constructions.

misconceptions.myth: Bhadrabāhu can be straightforwardly identified as the author of the Kalpa Sūtra, and this authorship is historically certain.
misconceptions.reality: The attribution of the Kalpa Sūtra to Bhadrabāhu is a respected Śvetāmbara tradition, but textual and chronological analysis suggests that the work, in its present form, is later than the period usually assigned to the śruta-kevalin Bhadrabāhu. Many scholars therefore treat the attribution as devotional or symbolic rather than as a firmly established historical fact, and they distinguish between the canonical text itself and the evolving tradition of its authorship.

misconceptions.myth: The famine and migration led by Bhadrabāhu directly and immediately caused the split between Digambara and Śvetāmbara sects.
misconceptions.reality: While southern narratives link Bhadrabāhu’s leadership during a twelve-year famine to a migration of monks and to later differences in practice, the formal Digambara–Śvetāmbara division crystallized centuries after Bhadrabāhu’s time. The famine story is one factor in a long, complex process of regional, doctrinal, and disciplinary differentiation, not a single decisive event that instantly created two separate sects.

misconceptions.myth: The story of Chandragupta Maurya becoming Bhadrabāhu’s disciple and undertaking saṃlekhana at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa is fully confirmed by independent historical evidence.
misconceptions.reality: This narrative is deeply cherished in Digambara tradition and supported by local inscriptions that commemorate Bhadrabāhu and Chandragupta together. However, non-Jain historical sources for Chandragupta’s life do not mention Bhadrabāhu or a Jain saṃlekhana at Śravaṇabeḷgoḷa. Historians therefore regard the story as a later hagiographical development that may preserve some historical memory of royal contact with Jainism but cannot be accepted in all its details as firmly established fact.

misconceptions.myth: Bhadrabāhu’s status as the last śruta-kevalin means that all earlier Jain scriptures were perfectly preserved and transmitted without loss until his time, and then suddenly disappeared.
misconceptions.reality: The designation of Bhadrabāhu as the last śruta-kevalin expresses a traditional awareness that mastery of the complete Pūrvas was gradually becoming rarer and eventually ceased. It does not imply a sharp, all-or-nothing transition. The loss and transformation of early Jain scriptural material was a long, uneven process, and the figure of Bhadrabāhu serves symbolically to mark the end of an idealized era of complete oral mastery rather than a single moment when the canon was abruptly lost.
